{{Short description|Russo-American physicist}}
[[File:Петр Питиримович Сорокин.jpg|thumb|Sorokin in 2015]]
'''Peter Pitirimovich Sorokin''' ({{langx|ru|Пётр Питиримович Сорокин}}, 10 July 1931 – 24 September 2015) was an [[Russian Americans|American Russian]] physicist and co-inventor of the [[dye laser]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Dye lasers|last=Schäfer|first=F. P.|publisher=Springer-Verlag|year=1990|editor-last=Schäfer|editor-first=F. P.|location=Berlin|chapter=Chapter 1: Principles of Dye Laser Operation|oclc=21561617|author-link=F. P. Schäfer}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Tunable Laser Optics|first=F. J.|publisher=[[CRC Press]]|year=2015|isbn=978-1-4822-4529-5|edition=2nd|location=New York|pages=1–30|chapter=Introduction to lasers|oclc=902838121|author-link=F. J. Duarte|last=Duarte}}</ref>  He was born in [[Boston]] and grew up in [[Winchester, Massachusetts]].<ref>''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Bethune|first1=Donald S.|last2=Wynne|first2=James J.|date=23 December 2015|title=Peter Pitirimovich Sorokin: Laser pioneer dedicated to understanding, creating, and using light|journal=[[Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]]|volume=113|issue=1|pages=12–3|doi=10.1073/pnas.1523215113|pmc=4711863|pmid=26699496|bibcode=2016PNAS..113...12B|doi-access=free}}</ref> He attended Harvard University, receiving a [[BA Degree|BA degree]] in 1952 and a [[PhD]] in [[Applied physics|Applied Physics]] in 1958; his PhD [[Doctoral advisor|thesis advisor]] was [[Nicolaas Bloembergen]].<ref name=":0" />

== Personal life ==
Peter Sorokin was a son of a prominent Russian sociologist [[Pitirim Sorokin]] and his wife Microbiologist Dr. [[Elena Baratynskaya]], who belonged to [[Russian nobility]] (see: {{ill|Baratynsky|ru|3=Баратынские}}). Sorokin died at the age of 84 on 24 September 2015 from injuries incurred in a fall in August.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
Sorokin joined [[IBM Research|IBM research labs]] in 1958.<ref name=":0" /> In 1960 the first laser, the [[ruby laser]], was developed at [[HRL Laboratories|Hughes Research Labs]] by [[Theodore Maiman]]. In 1962 Sorokin and Mirek Stevenson produced the second kind of laser using calcium fluoride doped with uranium.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sorokin |first=P. P. |last2=Stevenson |first2=M. J. |date=1960-12-15 |title=Stimulated Infrared Emission from Trivalent Uranium |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.5.557 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=5 |issue=12 |pages=557–559 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.5.557|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hecht |first=Jeff |date=2010-09-01 |title=Short history of laser development |url=https://opticalengineering.spiedigitallibrary.org/article.aspx?doi=10.1117/1.3483597 |journal=Optical Engineering |language=en |volume=49 |issue=9 |pages=091002 |doi=10.1117/1.3483597 |issn=0091-3286}}</ref>

Sorokin and his colleague J. R. Lankard, at IBM, used a ruby laser to excite a near infrared laser dye.  Their report was quickly followed by that of [[F. P. Schäfer]]. In 1974 Sorokin received the [[Albert A. Michelson Medal]] from the [[Franklin Institute]].<ref name="MichelsonMedal_Laureates">{{cite web |url=http://www.fi.edu/winners/show_results.faw?gs=&ln=&fn=&keyword=&subject=&award=MICH+&sy=1967&ey=1997&name=Submit |title=Franklin Laureate Database - Albert A. Michelson Medal Laureates |publisher=[[Franklin Institute]] |accessdate=June 14, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120406103546/http://www.fi.edu/winners/show_results.faw?gs=&ln=&fn=&keyword=&subject=&award=MICH+&sy=1967&ey=1997&name=Submit |archive-date=April 6, 2012 }}</ref> In 1983 Sorokin was awarded the [[Comstock Prize in Physics]] from the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]]<ref name="Comstock">{{cite web|title=Comstock Prize in Physics|url=http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_comstock|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|accessdate=13 February 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101229195326/http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_comstock|archive-date=29 December 2010}}</ref> and in 1984 the [[Harvey Prize]] from Israel's [[Technion]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.admin.technion.ac.il/harvey/ |title=The Harvey Prize |publisher=[[Technion]] |accessdate=August 9, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727092218/http://www.admin.technion.ac.il/harvey/ |archive-date=July 27, 2011 }}</ref> In 1991 he received the first [[Arthur L. Schawlow Prize in Laser Science]] from the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Arthur L. Schawlow Prize in Laser Science|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/schawlow.cfm|publisher=[[American Physical Society]]|accessdate=15 June 2011}}</ref> Sorokin became an [[IBM Fellow]] in 1968.<ref name="Femtosecond_Chemistry_Bio">{{Cite book | editor1-last = Manz | editor1-first = Jrn | editor2-first = Ludger | doi = 10.1002/9783527619436 | title = Femtosecond Chemistry | year = 1994 | isbn = 9783527619436 | editor2-last = Wste }} Look in chapter [http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/9783527619436.contrib/pdf Contributors’ CVs and Addresses] page 825.</ref>  He was also a [[OSA Fellow|Fellow of the Optical Society of America]]. Toward the end of his career he became interested in astronomy.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.lewisboroledger.com/28423/peter-p-sorokin-84-physicist/|title=Peter P. Sorokin, 84, physicist|date=28 September 2015|work=Lewisboro Ledger|department=Obituaries|location=Lewisboro, New York|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151001171807/http://www.lewisboroledger.com/28423/peter-p-sorokin-84-physicist/|archive-date=1 October 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>
